lead: This unit teaches how to build and evaluate regression and simple classification models. After reading you can fit a line, avoid over‑fitting and choose the best model for new data.
about: Unit 2 has seven chapters. 2.1 introduces linear regression by ordinary least squares for one and many variables. 2.2 shows how a loss function leads to batch and stochastic gradient descent. 2.3 covers logistic regression for binary classification. 2.4 extends linear decision functions to binary and multiclass discriminants. 2.5 explains over‑fitting, under‑fitting and the bias‑variance trade‑off. 2.6 adds ridge (L2) and lasso (L1) regularization. 2.7 finishes with cross‑validation, evaluation metrics and model selection. Each chapter builds on the previous one and connects to earlier units on foundations and classification.

chapters.idea: Fit a line or hyperplane by minimizing squared error.
chapters.depth: Derive the slope‑intercept formula for simple regression, write the normal equations, extend to matrix form for multiple regression, state the ordinary least squares name used in some syllabi, list assumptions (linearity, independence, constant variance).

figure.aria: Scatter points of phone price versus age with the fitted decreasing line.

chapters.example: A used phone loses ₹1000 each month. Age = 4 months. Predicted price = 11000 – 1000×4 = ₹7000.
chapters.trap: Omitting the intercept term gives a line forced through the origin.
chapters.prereq: Basic algebra and matrix multiplication; Unit 1 concepts.
chapters.leave: Polynomial regression and regularization are covered later.

chapters.idea: Iteratively update parameters opposite to the gradient of a loss.
chapters.depth: Define mean‑squared error loss, compute its gradient, describe batch gradient descent steps, introduce stochastic gradient descent with random mini‑batches, explain learning‑rate choice and convergence check. Some syllabi refer to this as stochastic gradient descent.

figure.title: Gradient Descent Loop
figure.aria: Block diagram showing the iterative steps of gradient descent.

chapters.example: Start w=0 for the phone data. Gradient = –2∑(y‑wx). With learning rate 0.01, first update w = 0 + 0.01×gradient = 0.45.
chapters.trap: Choosing a learning rate that is too large makes the loss increase.
chapters.leave: Momentum, Adam and other advanced optimizers are in later units.

chapters.idea: Predict class probabilities with a sigmoid of a linear score.
chapters.depth: Introduce sigmoid σ(z)=1/(1+e⁻ᶻ), derive log‑likelihood loss, compute its gradient, show decision threshold at 0.5, extend to one‑vs‑rest for multiple classes. Some syllabi call this a probabilistic discriminative model.

figure.aria: Sigmoid curve with a horizontal line at probability 0.5.

chapters.example: Transaction amount = ₹5000, time = 22h. Feature vector x=[5000,22]. Weight w=[0.0002,0.03]. Score z= w·x = 0.0002×5000+0.03×22=1+0.66=1.66. Probability = σ(1.66)=0.84 → classify as fraud.
chapters.trap: Using the raw score instead of the probability for the decision.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2 loss functions and gradient descent.
chapters.leave: Linear discriminant analysis and support vector machines are covered in Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Separate classes with a linear decision function.
chapters.depth: Define discriminant g(x)=w·x+b, give binary rule g(x)≥0, describe multiclass argmax rule, relate to perceptron algorithm mentioned in some syllabi, note that weights are learned by any of the previous optimization methods.

figure.aria: Flow from feature vector to discriminant computation to class selection.

chapters.example: Cricket score runs=150, wickets=4. Features x=[150,4]. Weights w₁=[0.02, -0.5] for class Low, w₂=[0.05, -0.2] for Medium, w₃=[0.08, 0.1] for High. Compute g₁=0.02×150-0.5×4=3-2=1, g₂=0.05×150-0.2×4=7.5-0.8=6.7, g₃=0.08×150+0.1×4=12+0.4=12.4 → class High.
chapters.trap: Using the same weight vector for all classes without one‑vs‑rest.
chapters.leave: Kernel tricks and maximum‑margin classifiers appear in Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Model error splits into bias, variance and irreducible noise.
chapters.depth: Define training error, test error, bias as error of average model, variance as variability around the average, draw the classic error‑vs‑complexity curve, discuss under‑fitting (high bias) and over‑fitting (high variance). Some syllabi list bias‑variance trade‑off.

figure.aria: Plot showing bias decreasing, variance increasing, and total error forming a U‑shape as complexity grows.

chapters.example: Fit polynomials of degree 1, 3 and 9 to house‑price points (₹). Degree 1 error=12k, degree 3 error=5k, degree 9 error=18k → shows under‑fit, good fit, over‑fit.
chapters.trap: Confusing high bias with low variance.
chapters.leave: Regularization techniques to control variance are in the next chapter.

chapters.idea: Add a penalty on coefficients to shrink them and reduce variance.
chapters.depth: Define ridge loss = MSE + λ∑w_j² (L2) and lasso loss = MSE + λ∑|w_j| (L1). Show ridge solution via (XᵀX+λI)⁻¹Xᵀy, describe coordinate descent for lasso. Note that only a few universities teach lasso in depth. Explain feature scaling before applying.

figure.aria: Lines showing how ridge shrinks coefficients smoothly while lasso drives some to zero as λ increases.

chapters.example: Multiple regression with features age, mileage. λ=1 gives ridge weights [2.3, 0.8]; λ=0.5 lasso gives [2.1, 0] → mileage dropped.
chapters.trap: Skipping feature standardization leads to uneven shrinkage.
chapters.leave: Choosing λ by cross‑validation is covered next.

chapters.idea: Estimate how a model will perform on unseen data and pick the best one.
chapters.depth: Explain train/validation/test split, k‑fold cross‑validation, leave‑one‑out, compute regression metrics RMSE = √(Σ(e²)/n) and MAE = Σ|e|/n, classification metrics accuracy, precision, recall, F1. Mention model selection terminology used in some syllabi.

figure.title: 5‑Fold CV Process
figure.aria: Block diagram showing the steps of 5‑fold cross‑validation.

chapters.example: Ridge regression λ=1 evaluated with 5‑fold CV gives RMSE values [4.2, 4.5, 4.1, 4.3, 4.4] → average RMSE = 4.3 ₹ thousand.
chapters.trap: Using test data during hyper‑parameter tuning leaks information.
chapters.leave: Ensemble methods and deep models are in later units.
